topics.title: Electric Current and Closed Electric Circuits

concepts.label: Electric Current and the Electric Circuit
concepts.cardText: If electric charge flows through a conductor such as a metallic wire, there is an electric current in it, just as flowing water makes a water current. In a torch, the cells provide the flow of charges through the bulb, which glows only when the switch is on. A switch makes a conducting link between the cell and the bulb. A continuous and closed path of an electric current is an electric circuit; if it is broken anywhere, the current stops and the bulb does not glow. Electric current is the amount of charge flowing through a particular area in unit time, the rate of flow of electric charges. In metallic wires electrons carry the charge, but conventionally the direction of current is taken opposite to the flow of electrons, because electricity was observed before electrons were known.

concepts.label: Measuring Current: Coulomb, Ampere and the Ammeter
concepts.cardText: If a net charge Q flows across any cross-section of a conductor in time t, the current is I = Q/t. The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C), the charge in nearly 6 × 10^18 electrons. Current is expressed in amperes (A): one ampere is the flow of one coulomb of charge per second, 1 A = 1 C/1 s. Small currents are expressed in milliampere and microampere. An instrument called an ammeter measures electric current in a circuit, and it is always connected in series. In a circuit, current flows from the positive terminal of the cell to the negative terminal through the bulb and ammeter.

concepts.label: Potential Difference: What Makes Charge Flow
concepts.cardText: Charges do not flow in a copper wire by themselves, just as water in a perfectly horizontal tube does not flow. If one end of the tube is connected to a tank at a higher level, the pressure difference makes water flow. For charges in a conducting wire the electrons move only if there is a difference of electric pressure, called the potential difference, along the conductor. It may be produced by a battery of one or more cells. The chemical action within a cell generates the potential difference across its terminals, even when no current is drawn. When the cell is connected to a conducting element, the potential difference sets the charges in motion and produces a current, and to maintain it the cell expends its stored chemical energy.

concepts.label: The Volt and the Voltmeter
concepts.cardText: The electric potential difference between two points in a current carrying circuit is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other: V = W/Q. The SI unit is the volt (V), named after Alessandro Volta. One volt is the potential difference between two points of a current carrying conductor when 1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb from one point to the other, so 1 V = 1 J per C. The potential difference is measured by an instrument called a voltmeter, which is always connected in parallel across the points between which the potential difference is to be measured. A circuit comprises a cell or battery, a plug key, components and wires, and is drawn as a schematic diagram using conventional symbols.

concepts.label: Ohm's Law: Potential Difference and Current
concepts.cardText: In an activity with a nichrome wire, an ammeter, a voltmeter and cells, the ratio V/I is approximately the same each time, and the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin: V/I is a constant ratio. In 1827 the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm found the relationship between the current flowing in a metallic wire and the potential difference across its terminals. The potential difference across the ends of a given metallic wire is directly proportional to the current flowing through it, provided its temperature remains the same. This is Ohm's law, V = IR, where R is a constant for the given wire at a given temperature, called its resistance.

concepts.label: Electrical Resistance, the Ohm and the Rheostat
concepts.cardText: Resistance is the property of a conductor to resist the flow of charges through it. Its SI unit is the ohm (Ω): if the potential difference across a conductor is 1 V and the current through it is 1 A, its resistance is 1 Ω. From Ohm's law, the current through a resistor is inversely proportional to its resistance; if the resistance is doubled, the current gets halved. A component that regulates current without changing the voltage source is a variable resistance, and a rheostat is often used to change the resistance in a circuit. Electrons are not completely free to move within a conductor; they are restrained by the attraction of the atoms among which they move. A good conductor of a given size offers low resistance, a resistor has appreciable resistance, and an insulator offers even higher resistance.

topics.title: Factors Affecting Resistance and Electrical Resistivity

concepts.label: Factors on Which the Resistance of a Conductor Depends
concepts.cardText: Experiments with nichrome and copper wires show that the ammeter reading decreases to one-half when the length of the wire is doubled, increases when a thicker wire of the same material and length is used, and changes when a wire of different material of the same length and cross-section is used. Applying Ohm's law, the resistance of a conductor depends on its length, its area of cross-section and the nature of its material. Precise measurements show that the resistance of a uniform metallic conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its area of cross-section: R = ρ l/A, where ρ (rho) is a constant of proportionality called the electrical resistivity of the material.

concepts.label: Electrical Resistivity and the Choice of Materials
concepts.cardText: Resistivity is a characteristic property of a material, with SI unit ohm metre. Metals and alloys have very low resistivity, in the range 10^-8 to 10^-6 ohm metre, and are good conductors; insulators like rubber and glass have resistivity of the order of 10^12 to 10^17 ohm metre. Both resistance and resistivity vary with temperature. The resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals, and alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures, so they are commonly used in electrical heating devices like electric irons and toasters. Tungsten is used almost exclusively for filaments of electric bulbs, whereas copper and aluminium are generally used for electrical transmission lines.

concepts.label: Resistors in Series: Current, Potential Difference and Equivalent Resistance
concepts.cardText: There are two methods of joining resistors. When resistors are joined end to end, they are connected in series. In a series combination the current is the same in every part of the circuit: the same current flows through each resistor, whatever the ammeter's position. The total potential difference across a series combination equals the sum of the potential differences across the individual resistors, V = V1 + V2 + V3. Applying Ohm's law gives the equivalent resistance: when several resistors are joined in series, the resistance of the combination equals the sum of the individual resistances, Rs = R1 + R2 + R3, and is thus greater than any individual resistance.

topics.title: Parallel Combination of Resistors and Domestic Circuits

concepts.label: Resistors in Parallel: Potential Difference, Currents and Equivalent Resistance
concepts.cardText: When resistors are connected together between two points X and Y, they are connected in parallel. The potential difference across each resistor in a parallel combination is the same as the potential difference across the whole combination. The total current is equal to the sum of the separate currents through each branch, I = I1 + I2 + I3, since each resistor carries V/R. Applying Ohm's law, the reciprocal of the equivalent resistance of a group of resistances joined in parallel is equal to the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances, so the equivalent resistance is smaller than any one of them.

concepts.label: Why Domestic Circuits Use Parallel Connections
concepts.cardText: In a series circuit the current is constant throughout, so it is impracticable to connect an electric bulb and an electric heater in series, because they need widely different currents to operate properly. Another major disadvantage is that when one component fails the circuit is broken and none of the components works, as with fairy lights, where the electrician has to test each bulb to find the dead one. A parallel circuit, on the other hand, divides the current through the electrical gadgets. The total resistance in a parallel circuit is decreased, which is helpful particularly when each gadget has a different resistance and requires a different current to operate properly.

topics.title: Heating Effect of Electric Current and Joule's Law of Heating

concepts.label: The Heating Effect of Electric Current and Joule's Law
concepts.cardText: A cell's chemical reaction generates the potential difference that sets electrons in motion, and to maintain the current the source keeps expending energy. A part may be consumed in useful work, like rotating the blades of a fan; the rest is expended as heat, so a fan becomes warm if used for long. If the circuit is purely resistive, the source energy is dissipated entirely as heat: the heating effect of electric current, used in the electric heater and iron. For a steady current I through a resistor R for time t, the heat produced is H = VIt, and with Ohm's law H = I²Rt. This is Joule's law of heating: the heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the square of the current for a given resistance, directly proportional to the resistance for a given current, and directly proportional to the time for which the current flows.

topics.title: Practical Applications of Heating Effects: Electric Fuse and Lighting

concepts.label: Applications of Joule Heating: Heaters, Bulb Filaments and Fuses
concepts.cardText: The generation of heat in a conductor is an inevitable consequence of electric current. It is often undesirable because it converts useful electrical energy into heat, but it has many useful applications: the electric iron, toaster, oven, kettle and heater are based on Joule heating. It is also used to produce light, as in an electric bulb, where the filament must retain as much heat as possible so that it gets very hot and emits light; tungsten, with a melting point of 3380 degrees Celsius, is used for filaments, which are thermally isolated and kept in chemically inactive nitrogen and argon to prolong life. A fuse is placed in series with the device and protects circuits and appliances by stopping unduly high current: if a current larger than the specified value flows, its wire melts and breaks the circuit. Fuses are rated 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A and so on; an iron using 1 kW at 220 V draws 4.54 A, so a 5 A fuse is used.

topics.title: Electric Power and Commercial Electrical Energy Consumption

concepts.label: Electric Power and the Commercial Unit of Energy
concepts.cardText: Power is the rate of doing work, which is also the rate of consumption of energy. The rate at which electric energy is dissipated or consumed in an electric circuit is electric power: P = VI = I²R = V²/R. The SI unit of electric power is the watt (W), the power consumed by a device that carries 1 A of current when operated at a potential difference of 1 V. In practice the much larger unit kilowatt, 1000 watts, is used. Since electrical energy is the product of power and time, its unit is the watt hour, the energy consumed when 1 watt of power is used for 1 hour. The commercial unit of electric energy is the kilowatt hour (kW h), commonly known as a 'unit', and 1 kW h = 3.6 × 10^6 joule. Electrons are not consumed in a circuit: we pay for the energy used to move them through gadgets.
